source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (intrinsic condition)
finding: With no outside signal, asking the model to re-check its answer made accuracy go down, not up. Earlier gains came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction, calls 1 then 3 then 5. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0.
limits: Prompted self-review only, no external check. Benchmarks are math and commonsense, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: A second look by the same model with no check has negative expected value. Supports G1 and G2: re-examine only on a code-located signal.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (oracle condition)
finding: When the true label told the loop when to revise, the same second-look prompt gave big gains. This is the source of the optimistic literature.
numbers: Oracle self-correction. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 -> 59.0.
limits: Oracle labels are not available in real diagnosis, so these are an upper bound.
agent_relevance: The value sits in the stop/continue signal, not in re-reading. S8 needs a real check, not a model opinion.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (answer-change analysis)
finding: Models cannot judge whether their own reasoning is right. When they change an answer they more often turn a right one into a wrong one.
numbers: GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time after two rounds. On CommonSenseQA it changes more, with a high correct-to-incorrect ratio. GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo keep initial answers more often. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 -> 43.5 -> 36.5; GPT-4-Turbo 91.5 -> 88.0 -> 90.0.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Stronger models change less, so they lose less but also gain less.
agent_relevance: Measure what the second look changed and whether the change was right. Keep the first answer unless a check fails.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Survey of self-correction work. No prior work shows success with feedback from a prompted model alone, except on tasks unusually suited to it. Reliable external feedback works. Large-scale fine-tuning also enables it.
numbers: Three headline conclusions; no paper counts read from the abstract. Reflexion with oracle feedback is listed as an unfair setting.
limits: Survey, not a new experiment. Many papers do not state their research question, so their setups over-credit self-correction.
agent_relevance: A second look pays where tools, tests, retrieval or executed code supply the feedback. This matches S5 with code-located failing output.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic Reasoning Prompts Reveal the Potential for LLM Interpretability in Medicine
finding: Prompting models to follow clinician reasoning styles (differential diagnosis, analytic, Bayesian, intuitive) did not help GPT-4 and hurt GPT-3.5. Copying human reasoning structure is not a free gain.
numbers: MedQA test set 518 (497 for GPT-4). GPT-3.5: traditional CoT 46%, intuitive 48%, analytic 40% (-6, p=0.001), differential 38% (-8, p<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4, p=0.02). GPT-4: CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78%, analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4, p=0.07).
limits: Multiple-choice MedQA, one pass, not a second look. Prompts developed on 95 training questions.
agent_relevance: A clinician-style reasoning step must be tested against plain CoT at equal tokens (G7). The best case is interpretability without accuracy loss.

source: Savage et al. (2023), GPT-4 effect sizes
finding: For GPT-4 no structured diagnostic prompt moved accuracy beyond noise. Listing a differential first was not enough when the model already reasons well.
numbers: GPT-4 differential diagnosis +2.2 points (CI -1.4 to +5.8, p=0.24); intuitive +0.8 (p=0.73); analytic +1.6 (p=0.35); Bayesian -3.4 (p=0.07). Inter-rater agreement 99%, kappa 0.98.
limits: Same data as c05; kept as a separate line because it bounds the size of a step-structure prompt effect.
agent_relevance: Expect null or single-digit effects from step structure alone; look for effects where a signal or outside check exists.

source: Medical QA study (2026) Can Large Language Models Self-Correct in Medical Question Answering? An Exploratory Study
finding: An iterative self-reflection loop (up to 10 steps) did not reliably beat plain chain of thought on three medical QA sets. The effect depends on dataset and model size.
limits: Zero-shot, black-box, exam multiple choice, no external check, one run. Gains of about one point are within noise at these n.
agent_relevance: A same-model critic loop is at best a tiny gain on clinical-reasoning exam items and a small loss on evidence-reading items. Do not add it as a default step.

source: Same study (2026), behaviour across reflection steps
finding: Most items stop after zero or one reflection. More steps do not accumulate benefit and make the smaller model unstable.
numbers: GPT-4o: over 85% of instances need no extra reflection on each dataset. MedQA has the deepest reflection for both models. GPT-4o-mini accuracy oscillates across steps on MedQA; PubMedQA curves are flat.
limits: Exploratory; error-corrected versus error-introduced counts appear only in figures.
agent_relevance: Cap rounds low (SCHEMA S5 says 2). Confident models rarely re-open, which fits G1.

source: Same study (2026), stop rule
finding: The loop let the model end reflection when it felt satisfied. That is the model-judged stop rule Huang et al. criticise.
numbers: K = 10 maximum steps; a majority vote over all steps was computed only when the model never reported satisfaction.
limits: No external-check arm or oracle arm, so the gap between model-judged and code-judged stopping is untested here.
agent_relevance: A direct test for our harness: same loop with a code-located trigger versus a model-judged trigger, equal tokens.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Seven human-style cognitive biases injected into USMLE questions cut accuracy. Models show the same slips clinicians show.
numbers: Clean accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7B 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-LLaMA-13B 33.4%. Drops of 10 to 26 points depending on model. GPT-4 worst case -14.0% (false consensus), confirmation only -0.2%. GPT-3.5 average -37.4%, worst case 23.9%. Mean over models: false consensus -24.9%, frequency -18.2%, recency -12.9%, confirmation -8.1%.
limits: Each bias is one injected sentence in a MedQA vignette; real cases are messier. Some models refused or did not answer.
agent_relevance: Strip or flag leading statements (a prior diagnosis, someone's opinion) at input. This is the S1 input hygiene case.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA, mitigation arms
finding: Warning the model about bias, or showing a biased example, recovered only part of the loss, mostly for GPT-4.
numbers: Bias education: GPT-4 frequency bias 0.627 -> 0.720. One-shot negative example: GPT-4 recency 0.679 -> 0.742. Few-shot (wrong plus right example): largest GPT-4 gains on status quo and recency. Other models gained marginally. Non-response 94.4% (one-shot) and 99.5% (few-shot) for PaLM-2 text-bison (safety filters).
limits: Authors call the gains modest. A generic warning is the machine analogue of 'be careful', which also helps people little.
agent_relevance: A generic 'beware of bias' line is cheap but weak. Prefer a concrete code-run counter-check, for example re-ask with the leading sentence removed and compare.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: A 13,465-prompt set tests anchoring, status quo, framing, group attribution and primacy bias in a high-stakes task (student admissions). Self-help debiasing, where the model rewrites the prompt to remove bias, worked without hand-made examples.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. Mitigation arms: self-awareness, contrastive, counterfactual few-shot, self-help. Exact effect sizes were not extracted.
limits: Not medical. I read the abstract and method, not every results table.
agent_relevance: Self-help debiasing edits the input, not the answer. It is the one machine analogue of a structured re-examination worth testing in S1 and S2.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning
finding: Models that must request data over three rounds under-request at the end. Fluent reasoning text does not predict accuracy.
numbers: 32 frontier models, 20 hematologic oncology cases. Best overall accuracy 68%. Information utilization correlates with accuracy R = 0.69 (p < 0.001). Utilization fell from about 57% in rounds 1 and 2 to 25.7% in round 3. Reasoning rubric above threshold (6 of 10) in 91% of evaluations while mean accuracy was 56.3%.
limits: One specialty, 20 cases, simulated data release.
agent_relevance: Reasoning text is not evidence (G10). A second look should ask what was not yet requested, and code should force it, since models stop asking by round 3.

source: VivaBench authors (2025) Simulating Viva Voce Examinations to Evaluate Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Moving from full information to interactive history, exam and tests, accuracy fell to about half or less. Failures looked like human cognitive errors.
numbers: 990 cases (934 evaluated), 6 models, temperature 0. Gemini 2.5 Pro: final top-1 0.35, full-information top-1 0.69, provisional top-1 0.17. o4-mini 0.32 vs 0.63. DeepSeek-R1 0.23 vs 0.61. Llama-4 Maverick 0.23 vs 0.52. LLM-classified failure causes: inappropriate hypothesis generation 348, premature diagnostic closure 291, inadequate investigations 90, ICD coding errors 9.
limits: Failure classes were assigned by an LLM classifier; the text has an unfilled 'X cases' placeholder. Published case reports may be in training data (authors found no exact matches in the top 10% by similarity).
agent_relevance: Premature closure is the second most common failure. A step that asks 'which finding would refute my leading diagnosis, have I looked for it' targets this. Test it by running, not by self-grading.

source: Active Evidence-Seeking and Diagnostic Reasoning in LLMs for Clinical Decision Support (2026)
finding: Multi-turn evidence gathering with a simulated patient lowered accuracy and evidence quality versus having the whole case at once. Authors link this to premature closure and weak questions.
numbers: 468 cases, 15 models. Mean exact accuracy -12.75 points and supporting-evidence quality -24.36% from full-context to active task. Gemini-2.5-Pro 65.20% in full context. Baichuan-M1-14B 42.5 -> 34.0; Qwen3-8B 53.4 -> 39.5; Llama-3-8B 37.0 -> 23.3.
limits: Simulated patient. Single reference diagnosis. Text only.
agent_relevance: Static benchmarks overstate what a loop achieves. Measure S5 and S8 with progressive disclosure where possible.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning, JAMA Netw Open
finding: Giving physicians GPT-4 did not improve their diagnostic reasoning score, but GPT-4 alone scored higher than the doctors. People did not turn the model into a good second look on their own case.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), 244 cases. Median score 76% (IQR 66-87) with LLM vs 74% (63-84) conventional, adjusted difference 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, p=.60). LLM alone 92% (82-97), 16 points above conventional (95% CI 2-30, p=.03). Time 519 s vs 565 s (difference -82 s, CI -195 to 31).
limits: Read through a fetch summary; the last about 10k characters were not read. Article does not report whether doctors revised their diagnosis after seeing LLM output.
agent_relevance: A strong model alone beat the human-plus-model pair. A review step must not hand the final choice to a weaker party.

source: Characterizing Rhetorical Misalignment in Decision-Making with Language Models (2026)
finding: Readers with medical background changed answers after reading model text. Some changes went from correct to wrong, and written reasons point to anchoring, authority bias and loss aversion.
numbers: 939 annotations from 162 participants (Prolific, self-reported medical training), USMLE items. Accuracy 45.7% before and 57.5% after reading AI information. Average answer change rate 27.58%; average harmful flip (correct to incorrect) 2.81%.
limits: Self-reported training; text-only vignettes.
agent_relevance: Confident wording in a second-look text pulls the reader. Judges and the review step should see neutral, length-normalised text without a stated answer (G5).

source: Cognitive bias in LLM reasoning compromises interpretation of clinical oncology notes (2025)
finding: GPT-4 chain-of-thought on real oncology notes contained reasoning errors that map onto cognitive biases. Automated detectors found that an error existed but could not reliably name its type.
numbers: 23.1% (plus or minus 0.8) of interpretations had errors; reasoning failures 85.4% of errors; 600 annotated traces; validation 822 responses from prostate notes with error rate 27.4% (plus or minus 1.2). Among erroneous validation responses (n=129) reasoning failures 96.7%; confirmation bias 25.2% of tier-3 errors. Inter-rater agreement 0.85 (kappa 0.87 to 0.89 across tiers).
limits: One model (GPT-4), oncology notes only; labels by human annotators.
agent_relevance: A checker can flag that something is wrong, but naming the cause is weak. S5 should cite the failing output, not a cause label.

source: Nair et al. (2023) DERA: Enhancing LLM Completions with Dialog-Enabled Resolving Agents
finding: A two-agent loop (Researcher flags issues, Decider revises) improved GPT-4 on clinical summaries and care plans by physician judgment, but gave no gain on open-ended MedQA.
numbers: Summaries: physicians chose DERA over initial GPT-4 90% to 10%; 'All' relevant information captured 86% vs 56%; harmful content 2% -> 0%; physicians agreed with all Researcher suggestions in 63% of encounters, none in 18%. Care plans: DERA preferred 84% to 16%; complete 92% vs 64%. Open-ended MedQA: GPT-4 about 70%, DERA similar.
limits: Free-text generation graded by physicians; for answer selection the loop did not help.
agent_relevance: The second look helps completeness (what was left out) more than correctness of one answer. Use it as a missing-item audit, not a verdict step.

source: Tang et al. (2023) MedAgents: LLMs as Collaborators for Zero-shot Medical Reasoning
finding: A role-play consultation loop (analysis, summary, discussion, revision) beat plain CoT on medical QA. Most of the gain came from the first step.
numbers: MedQA ablation (GPT-3.5): direct 49.0, CoT 55.0, role-playing agents 62.0 (+7.0 over CoT), plus analysis 65.0, plus summary 67.0. MedAgents with GPT-4: MedQA 83.7, MedMCQA 74.8. Error analysis of 40 failures: 77% knowledge confusion or missing or wrong retrieval.
limits: Gains over CoT are partly extra compute; equal-call comparison is not shown for every set.
agent_relevance: Most failures are knowledge gaps, not reasoning slips, so a second look cannot fix them without new information (G2). Compare against equal-call voting (G7).

source: Kim et al. (2024) MDAgents: An Adaptive Collaboration of LLMs for Medical Decision-Making
finding: Choosing the amount of collaboration by case difficulty beat fixed solo or group setups. A final moderator review added accuracy.
numbers: Average accuracy 71.8% baseline; with moderator review 77.6% (+8.1%); with MedRAG 75.2% (+4.7%); both 80.3% (+11.8%). Best on 7 of 10 medical benchmarks. Group beat solo on some sets (91.9% vs 88.7%).
limits: Percent changes are relative per paper's notation. Retrieval confounds the review effect.
agent_relevance: Spend by difficulty (G12). The review adds value when paired with new evidence from retrieval.

source: Tu et al. (2024) Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI (AMIE)
finding: AMIE ran a three-step chain at each turn: analyse the case and current differential, write the reply, then revise the reply against factuality and format criteria. It beat primary care physicians on specialist-rated differential accuracy in a text OSCE.
numbers: 20 board-certified PCPs, 20 patient actors, 149 scenarios. AMIE top-k accuracy higher than PCPs for every k (p<0.05, bootstrap 10,000, FDR corrected). PCP differentials averaged 5.39 diagnoses (min 3); AMIE up to 10. Self-play inner loop used in-context critic feedback; 613 common conditions x4 and 4,617 less common x2 dialogues.
limits: Gain comes from fine-tuning plus self-play plus the chain; no ablation isolates the revise step. Simulated patients, text chat. PCPs gave shorter lists, which affects top-k.
agent_relevance: A shipped refine step inside an agent loop, but its criteria are style and factuality, not hypothesis testing.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: An agent writes a short verbal lesson after a failed attempt and retries with it in memory. It works where the environment gives a clear pass or fail signal.
numbers: Absolute gains: AlfWorld +22% in 12 learning steps, HotPotQA +20%, HumanEval up to +11%.
limits: Depends on a reliable outcome signal (tests, game reward); authors note code agents are bound by test quality. Huang et al. note the QA setup used oracle labels.
agent_relevance: Reflect on a failed test is the right S5. Reflect on one's own confidence is not.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: One model drafts, critiques and refines. It helps on generation tasks with clear quality aspects.
numbers: GPT-4 + Self-Refine on Code Optimization 27.3% -> 36.0% (+8.7 absolute). Seven tasks across dialogue, code, math, sentiment reversal.
limits: Gains on subjective or style tasks judged partly by models; weaker on reasoning tasks per Huang et al.
agent_relevance: Fits writing quality, not single-answer correctness. Not a basis for S8.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Verification by search or code interpreter, then correction, beats self-only critique. Self-verification alone gave modest gains or harm.
numbers: ChatGPT: +7.7 F1 over three QA tasks, +7.0% absolute over three math tasks, 79.2% lower toxicity probability. Also tested Text-Davinci-003 and LLaMA-2 7B, 13B, 70B.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Needs tools. Not medical.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S4 and S8: check by execution or retrieval, then revise. The diagnosis analogue is a guideline lookup or a lab-value calculation run by code.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in LLMs
finding: Plan verification questions, answer them independently of the draft, then revise. Answering them separately from the draft (factored) beats joint answering.
numbers: Wikidata list precision 0.17 -> 0.36 (Llama 65B). MultiSpanQA F1 0.39 -> 0.48 (+23%). Longform FACTSCORE 55.9 -> 71.4 (+28%); factored vs joint 60.8 -> 63.7.
limits: Factual recall, not diagnosis. Llama 65B baseline is weak.
agent_relevance: The closest published form of a structured second look: verification questions must not see the draft answer. Matches G5 blindness.
